etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin initiātus, perfect passive participle of initiō (“begin, originate”), from initium (“a beginning”), from ineō (“go in, enter upon, begin”), from in + eō (“go”).

definitions.definition: A new member of an organization.
One who has been through a ceremony of initiation.
One who is oriented in and familiar with a topic or subject; especially, one who is an expert in it.

quote.citation: 1860, Isaac Taylor, “(please specify the page)”, in Ultimate Civilization and Other Essays, London: Bell and Daldy […], →OCLC:
quote.text: How are changes of this sort to be initiated?

quote.citation: 1978, David Dhlalangami Maforo, Black-white Relations in Kenya Game Policy, page 5:
quote.text: Indigenous people, such as agriculturists, hunters, and pastoralists initiated a system of totemism and tabooism which in essence was a natural law against killing and eating certain animals.

quote.citation: 2011, Jim Baggott, The First War of Physics, Pegasus Books, →ISBN:
quote.text: A U235 bomb would therefore need to incorporate a gun weighing ten tons. Then there was the question of initiating or triggering the bomb.

quote.citation: 2014, David L. Elliott, Ultraviolet Laser Technology and Applications, page 320:
quote.text: Prior to firing the laser, a surgeon can preilluminate the area to be cut or ablated, enlarge or reduce the area, shape, or size, and then initiate the UV laser pulses for the actual ablation.

quote.citation: 2021 February 24, Encyclopedia of Virology, Academic Press, →ISBN, page 43:
quote.text: With the exception of anelloviruses, bidnaviruses, spiraviruses, and some inoviruses, the replicative protein of ssDNA viruses is the so-called HUH endonuclease that cuts genomic DNA at a specific site and initiates rolling circle (or rolling hairpin) replication.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To instruct in the rudiments or principles; to introduce.

quote.citation: 1653, Henry More, An Antidote against Atheisme, or An Appeal to the Natural Faculties of the Minde of Man, whether There Be Not a God, London:  […]  Roger Daniel, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Divine Providence would only initiate and enter mankind into the useful knowledge of her, leaving the rest to employ our industry.

quote.citation: 1693, [John Locke], “§94”, in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: to initiate his pupil in any part of learning

definitions.definition: (transitive) To confer membership on; especially, to admit to a secret order with mysterious rites or ceremonies.

quote.citation: 1738–1741, William Warburton, The Divine Legation of Moses […], volume (please specify |volume=I, II.1, or II.2), London:  […]  Fletcher Gyles, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The Athenians believed that he who was initiated and instructed in the mysteries would obtain celestial honour after death.

quote.citation: 1714 August 15 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison], “WEDNESDAY, August 4, 1714”, in The Spectator, number 576; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume VI, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: He was initiated into half a dozen clubs before he was one and twenty.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To do the first act; to perform the first rite; to take the initiative.

quote.citation: 1725–1726, Homer, “Book 3”, in [William Broome, Elijah Fenton, Alexander Pope], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC:
quote.text: The king himself initiates to the power; Scatters with quivering hand the sacred flour, And the stream sprinkles.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv]:
quote.text: the initiate fear that wants hard use

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Begun; commenced; introduced to, or instructed in, the rudiments; newly admitted.

quote.citation: 1744, [Edward Young], “Night the Sixth. The Infidel Reclaim’d. In Two Parts. Containing, the Nature, Proof, and Importance of Immortality. Part the First. […]”, in The Complaint: Or, Night-Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality, London:  […]  R[obert] Dodsley […], →OCLC, page 6:
